subject: how to incorporate inequality restrictions in residual variances and covariances

messages.author: e86f147b1255a868
messages.subject: how to incorporate inequality restrictions in residual variances and covariances
parts:
Dear all

I am dealing with a huge model with more than 700 parameters, 146 observed variables, 28 latent variables, one of them affecting all observed variables and the rest affecting only between 8 and 15 variables, some latent variables are orthogonal and others can correlate, all variances fixed to 1, and a sample of 1500 data. After 3000 iterations and once the computation has used all my 8Gb! ram memory I get the corresponding message and the result shows that for example residual variances of the observed variables exceed the initial variances and no regression coefficients at all (all 0). Is there a way to incorporate inequality restrictions on the residual variances, like they can´t exceed observed variances, as to fix the estimation process to a subset and by this trying to avoid my problem in the estimation (maybe this helps!)?

Thanks a lot in advance
Michael

I am not surprised. R (and lavaan) are very hungry for memory. Are you
dealing with categorical data? Or is everything continuous?

If you have categorical data, try using the current dev version
(0.5-17.697) which is already much more efficient for categorical data.

> I get the corresponding message and the result shows that for example
> residual variances of the observed variables exceed the initial
> variances and no regression coefficients at all (all 0). Is there a way
> to incorporate inequality restrictions on the residual variances, like
> they can´t exceed observed variances, as to fix the estimation process
> to a subset and by this trying to avoid my problem in the estimation
> (maybe this helps!)?

Well, ou can label all the residual variances, eg

item1 ~~ v1*item1

and then you can add inequality constraints, like:

v1 < 2.5

where '2.5' is, say, the initial variance.

But I don't think this will help a bit. I would break it down in smaller
pieces, estimate those pieces separately, and then use these values as
starting values for the larger model.

Yves.
